utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Up until October 1995, I was working as a clerk in the Zvornik Brigade. Excuse me, this was up until just before the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So before the war was ended in the area of Zvornik, a manoeuvring unit was formed as part of the Drina Corps and you joined that corps.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. A manoeuvring brigade was formed, which was headquartered in Kozluk, as I said, and I joined the brigade as assistant for operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at that post until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, until April 1996 I was at that post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your rank, Mr. Maric, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: I held the rank of captain or captain 1st class, I don't remember. Because that rank, captain 1st class, was later abolished. But I think I was captain 1st class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point I would like to ask you: When did you meet Dragan Jokic first?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: I first met Dragan Jokic when I arrived at the Zvornik Brigade; that is, in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did he occupy then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Dragan Jokic was then Chief of Engineers in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, in the summer of 1993, was there an Engineers Company in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: There was an Engineers Company in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher now, I would like to show this witness the exhibit we used yesterday; namely, a part of Richard Butler's report, Prosecution Exhibit 367, marked by us for identification as D84/3. I would kindly ask that it be put on the overhead projector and zoomed in, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, if you could assist us to understand the structure of the Zvornik Brigade and the various competencies and authority of different officers. In July 1993, who was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade? Or rather, July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: It was Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who occupied the post of deputy commander and at the same time Chief of Staff of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Major Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the brigade commander have its own staff of assistants?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had. Those were Assistant for Logistics, Sreten Milosevic; Assistant Commander for Morale and Religion, Nenad Simic; and there was also Chief of Security, 2nd Lieutenant Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These five officers, functionally speaking. Did they constitute the inner circle of command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. These officers were the innermost circle of command in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that month, was there in operation a Main Staff or headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that month as well there was a staff in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who headed that staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: The staff of the Zvornik Brigade was led by the Chief of Staff, Major Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you assist us with the composition of that staff in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: The staff of the Zvornik Brigade included ex officio the Assistant Commander for Operations, Major Miodrag Dragutinovic; the Assistant Commander for Personnel and Organisation, Mihajlo Galic; Assistant Commander for Intelligence, Dusko Vukotic; the commander of Staff Command or Staff Commander -- I can't recall the name now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, Mr. Maric. If you don't recall the name now, maybe you will remember it later.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Chiefs of Arms and Services, Artillery, Dragan Jokic; Chief of Communications, Milosav Petrovic. I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. There was Milenko Jovanovic, Staff Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one clarification for the record. I was advised by my colleague that I should repeat my question. Who was Chief of Engineers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was not Chief of Artillery; he was Chief of Engineers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now try to focus on the organ to which you belonged, led by Mr. Petkovic. What were its duties and what were its personnel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: The job of the operations staff in the Zvornik Brigade was to take part in the planning, organisation, documentation for combat operations, preparation of analyses and reports based on these documents, planning and organising internal services within the command and within units. And as for the staffing, in addition to the Assistant Commander for Operations there were several clerks or officers including me: Major Ljubo Bojanovic, Major Zoran Jovanovic, Captain Radenko Petrovic, Captain Momo Vasiljevic. So there were four or five of us clerks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the operations organ was the one who was preparing documents for the Chief of Staff, such as reports, combat documents, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Following instructions from the Chief of Staff, the operations section prepared these documents in keeping with the rules governing work in the army, which means that we would draft these documents, submit them to the Chief of Staff for endorsement, and they would later be submitted for final approval to the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that month, in July 1995, did the command and staff of the Zvornik Brigade operate according to those rules of the brigade and rules of staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The command of the brigade and the brigade indeed operated according to these military rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we say that it was an organised military formation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, could you assist us in clarifying the exact role of these heads of arms and services. What were their duties and tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Every head of a branch or service is in himself a technical, professional organ suggesting appropriate use of his units to the commander, taking part in the training of personnel, taking care that all the equipment be in working order, preparing documents, analyses, briefs, reports concerning his own units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can a chief or head of arms and services have a control-and- command function?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Control is a broader term, whereas command, as one of the elements of control, is not a role that the Chief of Engineers, for instance, has. According to the rules, it was only the commander of a unit who could command his unit, and this indeed happened in practice as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could a unit commander use his unit circumventing the commander without informing him, without obtaining his approval? Or can such use be made only with the approval of the commander, on his orders?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: A unit commander cannot put his unit to any kind of use without an appropriate order from the commander. That never happened in practice. When a unit commander receives an order from the commander, he must execute that order. If he wishes to discuss the best way to organise, he can consult with the commander and the chief of that particular branch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to find out. In that system of command and control, in an engineer's company, from the brigade commander through the Chief of Staff and commander of the Engineers Unit, what is the role of the Chief of Engineering?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Engineering or Engineers is an advisory organ suggesting appropriate use for engineers. His job is to take care that the personnel is well trained, that the equipment is in good working order, and that everything is combat-ready. His further role could be to take part in the preparation of all combat documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the commander required to follow the advice of his Chief of Arms and Services or Chief of Branch or can he act at his own discretion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: The commander is not duty-bound to take this advice. He doesn't even have to ask for advice if he has little time to make a decision. This happened very frequently, and the commander made decisions on his own. If he did have the time, he would consult the innermost circle of his assistants and make a decision accordingly. He was not therefore duty-bound to ask for advice and to follow it. He could decide on his own on how to use a particular unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point you said in some situations - and these situations occurred frequently - the commander could issue orders without consulting his assistants. What kind of situations are you referring to when a commander issues orders directly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: These are situations in which a large number of his assistants are not physically present, they are dislocated somewhere, and situations where there is not enough time for him to hear various proposals. In such situations, the commander assesses the situation quickly and makes a decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would a wartime situation where there is intense fighting and major battles going on be such a situation in which a commander may require the use of an engineers unit without consulting the Chief of Engineers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. Intensive fighting, changes in the combat situations on the ground requires fast decision-making, and this is how the commander would act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Another -- just one more question in this line of questioning: Would it be possible for any of the chiefs of arms of service to control units akin to his own? And this implies the use of machinery, vehicles, and so on, without the support of the commander logistically. Would the Chief of Engineers have such authority?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: No, the Chief of Engineers would not have the authority to command and issue orders to a unit, nor did this happen. What did happen was for the commander to send the chief of an arm of service to be with a unit for purposes of control and coordination in the implementation of orders issued by the commander, and this happened quite often. He would send the Chief of Signals with a signals unit in a particular combat operation. He would send the Chief of Engineers to be present during the mining or laying down minefields. But for the chief of a service to make a use on his own to his unit and issue such an order, this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please clarify this for us. The assistants to the commander that you mentioned, the Assistant for Logistics, the Assistant for Morale, the Assistant for Security. In terms of hierarchy, were they superior to the chief of an arm of service, functionally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, functionally speaking, they were superior to all the staff officers. They were assistants to the commander, responsible to the commander, while the other commanding officers I have listed would be responsible to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the hierarchy, the three assistants, could they be termed senior, establishment-wise, to the chiefs of arms of service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were senior, not according to rank but according to their function. Yes. As the word itself says, they are assistants to the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Maric, I want to put a few questions to you concerning the personality of Dragan Jokic. You told us that you met him in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what your impressions were of him as a person and in terms of his position in the structure of the brigade. What kind of authority did he have?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: When I first arrived in the Zvornik Brigade, Dragan Jokic was the Chief of Engineers. I learned later on that he was also the chief of the brigade. He was not an ambitious officer. He was not intent on pursuing a military career. I think that the role of Chief of Engineers was a kind of demotion for him because previously he had been Chief of Staff. The superior commander and the chief did not respect him very much. They did not take his opinions into account, so that many times attempts were made to keep him at a distance when certain activities were taking place, while on the other hand, his men respected him and thought well of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, the witness testified that - I quote - "I learned later on he was also the chief of the brigade." I have some questions on that. Would you please clarify this for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will attempt to do so through some questions, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, at one point in your response you said that you learnt in 1993 that Dragan Jokic for a time had been the Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Through my conversations with other colleagues, when we chatted I learned that numerous commanders and chiefs of staff had been at the head of the Zvornik Brigade before my arrival, and I think that Dragan Jokic had also had the role of Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade while its headquarters was still somewhere -- I think it was in 1992/1993. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this why you said that you understood that his position as Chief of Engineers was a demotion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say by this that the position of Chief of Staff is far more important than that of a staff officer such as Chief of Engineers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. The Chief of Staff is the second ranking, the second-in-command, while the Chief of Engineers is a demotion compared to that. It's going down to a far lower level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your direct contacts during 1995 with other officers in the staff, did you ever come to a conclusion why Dragan Jokic was marginalised in this way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just 1995. I think that Dragan Jokic sought to remove himself from positions of responsibility because the commander and the chief did not assign any important tasks to him. They gave him tasks that would demote him, embarrass him in front of his men. On several occasions he went with me and the units to oversee de-mining or the laying of minefields, and in essence the tasks assigned to him were such that he had to be with a small group of men and this was done to humiliate him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The attitude of Dragan Obrenovic as Chief of Staff to Dragan Jokic, was it the one you've described? In other words, that he did not take him seriously, take his opinions into account, that he undervalued his knowledge and skills and abilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic, the chief, did not like people who he thought were wise guys. When Dragan Jokic tried to explain something, he would say, "Oh, I've had enough of your lectures." He didn't like taking suggestions from others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic and Vinko Pandurevic, were they men of authority? Did they have sufficient strength and authority to be leaders of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: They were extremely capable officers. They had a great deal of authority, both with officers and with men and with the civilian authorities on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of age and rank, was Dragan Obrenovic younger than Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was much younger in terms of age. As for rank, I think he was a major and that he advanced in his career by two or three ranks from the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say that this was an autocratic, strong, powerful, authoritative officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic was an ambitious officer, capable, young. He wanted to prove himself. He saw a military career ahead of him, and he wanted to pursue that. He was exceptionally brave and was respected both by the officers and the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric, for this detailed information regarding the functional and personal status of Mr. Jokic. I would now like to go back and go through all of these dramatic days in mid-July 1995. And could you please help us by describing all these events, your position, and what you know about Dragan Jokic. Mr. Maric, do you remember that day when Srebrenica fell, which is what we use to describe that event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: This was on the 11th of July, 1995. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you were at the time and what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: I remember I was at the Zvornik Brigade Command in my office and in the duty operations room. I was in the section where the brigade command was. I was doing my usual things. We received these reports. There were many family members of fighters who were killed at Srebrenica. It was quite crowded and this went on until the next day also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there were families there of those who were killed in Srebrenica. Does that mean that a part of the Zvornik Brigade was in the Srebrenica sector during those several days?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Some of the forces of the Zvornik Brigade, with the commander Vinko Pandurevic, went on an assignment for combat operations in Srebrenica. I don't know exactly, but I think from the 4th to the 6th of July the unit left to carry out its assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the commander left with that group from the unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vinko Pandurevic was in command of that unit, and he went together with them for this task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it is logical to ask who then took over the command of the Zvornik Brigade during the absence of Commander Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: During the line-up of the unit which was preparing to leave for this assignment, to leave for Srebrenica, Vinko Pandurevic announced that the unit was going to carry out an assignment in Srebrenica and that in his absence the Chief of Staff, Major Dragan Obrenovic, should be in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this an official transfer of authority from Vinko Pandurevic to Dragan Obrenovic in terms of the command of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: This address by the commander we understood just as you have said it; it was an official transfer of authority, although according to the regulations, if the commander is not in the area of defence of the brigade, the authority is automatically transferred to his deputy or -- i.e., the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those few days, did you note the fact that Dragan Obrenovic was functionally de facto and de jure in command of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Right from the departure of Vinko Pandurevic, that's how it was. This was implemented in practice. Dragan Obrenovic commanded the units of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the operations officer, can you tell us, can you remember how many soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade left together with the commander to the Srebrenica sector?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: About 200 to 250 soldiers left with the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you find out that soldiers of Republika Srpska entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: We found this out on the 11th. I think it was in the duty operations officer's room. We found out that Srebrenica fell in the evening. We watched television, and we heard it also from our logistics section, how the combat operations were proceeding. We had the names of those who were killed and wounded, because all of that was then the duty of certain officers in the brigade to deal with all of these matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can recall, tell us where you spent the night between the 11th and the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: On the night of the 11th and 12th, I was at the command of the Zvornik Brigade. That's where I slept. We have a dormitory upstairs. I was in my office. I was in the duty operations room. We were monitoring the situation following what was happening with our units on the ground. I was also getting ready to be the officer on duty the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on the 12th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: On the 12th I took over as duty operations officer, between 8.00 and 9.00 hours. I acquainted myself with the situation in the brigade's area of defence. And then I continued with my duties as the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long is the shift of a duty operations officer, in general?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: According to the rules and also in practice, the shift -- the duty shift was 24 hours, which means 8.00 or 9.00 -- from 8.00 or 9.00 hours in the morning to 8.00 or 9.00 hours the following day, continuously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who you took over the duty from on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but when I looked at the handwriting in the duty handover logbook, I could conclude that the -- that based on the information I had, it was Ljubo Bojanovic. It was his handwriting before mine in the logbook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hand over your duty to on the 13th in the morning? Who came after you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: On the 13th, I handed over my duty to Sreten Milosevic, who was the Assistant Commander for Logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, Mr. Maric, was it usual and did this happen in the Zvornik Brigade that the deputy commander for security ever performed the duty of duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, the deputy chief for security was never the duty operations officer in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the security people ever do such duty in the brigade, due to the nature of the work that they do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: According to the manual of work of the military police, they can be on duty in their organ. They should always be available to assist the commander or the chief, so they never actually perform the duty operations job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness excerpts from the Manual of the Work of Commands and Staffs, and this is P394, and for identification we use that as D87/3. We will only look at the relevant articles from Rules 65 and 66, from the Manual of the Work of the Commands and Staffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, in view of the fact that in Dragan Jokic's indictment the -- his work as an operations officer is mentioned, I would like to ask you a few questions on this topic. How is the takeover -- the handover of duty carried out? How is this organised in the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: The officer who is taking over the duty usually comes early to prepare. He comes about half an hour to an hour earlier to prepare, to look at the documents, to acquaint himself with what happened the previous day, to see where the units were at that time, which actions were started, which ones were not implemented, to look over the duty-handover notebook, to see what was entered in it by his predecessor. The person take over the duty signs the book, as well as the person handing over the duty. This is monitored by the commander or certified by the commander. If he's not here, this is done by the Chief of Staff. It would happen sometimes in the absence of the commander and the Chief of Staff, who were not there during the takeover of the duty. When they were not in the barracks, then in the morning they would instruct for the duty operations officers to hand over duty by themselves, and they would then find out about what had happened from the duty operations officer once they returned to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the handover of duty from one duty officer -- the outgoing duty operations officer and the incoming one should always be approved or certified by the commander or the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: That is correct. At the beginning of each month a roster of duty is made by the officers in the brigade which is approved by the commander and the duty operations officers have to sign this schedule so they know who is on duty when, to prevent someone not being present or being on sick leave or being out in the field and being unable to come back. So any possible changes or substitutions could be made only with the approval of the commander and from the list of those who are supposed to be on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can it happen that duty operations officers substitute for one another without the knowledge of the commander or the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: No, this cannot happen. If the person who was supposed to take over the duty is not there, the person who was already on duty would continue to do so until a person approved by the commander to replace him turns up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a book in the Zvornik Brigade recording the handover of duty? Was there a notebook where an outgoing and an incoming duty operations officer would sign off, according to the approval of the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a notebook, and it was regularly maintained. Each shift would be noted down. Everything was written down in accordance with the regulations. The outgoing duty operations officer would sign it and the incoming one would also sign it, and this would be certified or authorised by the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information about what happened with this notebook of the handover of duty in the brigade? Did you have an opportunity later to see this notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: I saw the notebook in the hands of the Chief of Staff when he was preparing to conduct a defence. I think this was between his two interviews with investigators of the Hague Tribunal. I saw it in his office when he called me for a talk, amongst other thing, because he was preparing his defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, could you please tell us, could you please tell the Trial Chamber, what year was this when you saw this document, when you saw Mr. Obrenovic with this notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think this was in 1990 -- something like that. It was -- I think it was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 12th in the morning, when you were taking over the duty, was Obrenovic present in order to approve this handover of duty?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I took over the duty in the presence of Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please look at Rule 66 now, where instructions are -- on the work of commands and staffs are enumerated and where the operations duty officers' duties are also mentioned. Could you please tell us: As operations duty officer, what were you obliged to do on that day in the Zvornik Brigade? What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: The brigade duty officer needs to monitor the course of combat operations and to enter changes in the working map of the staff, to monitor what the neighbours are doing -- its neighbours are doing, to inform the commander or the Chief of Staff about any major events that are going on in the zone, or about orders received from a superior. The duty officer has to be acquainted with the disposition of the unit, all the elements of the units: Where the units were deployed; to control and maintain communications with the superior and -- command and subordinates; to receive and dispatch orders and reports to those to whom those orders and reports are addressed; to monitor and check the immediate security measures in the barracks, also at the command post. These are the rules for the work of a duty officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, as the duty officer, did you abide by those rules? And I'm now speaking specifically about the period of July 1995 in the Zvornik Brigade Command.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: I did abide by all of these rules, because I performed the duty officer function many times, so for me it was a routine. We mostly worked on duty. We organised it. We prepared for it. We also trained people for it. We also developed all the operational documents used for those purposes, and also in practice we abided by all of these rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be said that you were one of the most qualified people to work as duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Since I did this before the war, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, can you help us understand. What books did you have to keep as duty operations officer? In other words, out of all those diaries, notebooks, logbooks, what did you have at the command, at the command's duty operations centre?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: We had the book of transition of duty, the one that I spoke a moment ago [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the book that you said you saw in 1999 in Obrenovic's possession?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then we had a book of comments and observations, where the duty officer would note down what was going on; something like a working notebook, where everything that happened on a particular day was recorded chronologically and which is later used as a basis for compiling a final report. Those are the two main documents that I kept. Plus the duty operations officer always updates certain command-related documents regarding changes of codes, working map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who kept this war diary, Mr. Maric, the war journal kept in every brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, foundation. I don't know if any -- if what he's referred to is a war diary or if -- so I don't know -- There's no foundation to that question, so we don't know what he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please give us an explanation about the so-called war diary or just a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Maybe I hastened things a little, but I'll improve. I promise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, was there also a war journal at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Every unit in wartime keeps a war journal. It's not anybody's prerogative in particular, but in view of the substance it would have been normally the job of the operations organ in the brigade. All elements are updated every day chronologically. Every unit had to have this. And the same is true of the Zvornik Brigade, which had its war journal. In our command, there was a major, a teacher of fine arts by profession, otherwise a reserve major who served in the workers battalion officially, but he worked at the command of the brigade. He was an elderly man with an extremely beautiful handwriting and he was the one who kept this war journal precisely because he had this calligraphic handwriting. He would be given appropriate data and enter them into the war journal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that this was the job of the operations organ to keep this book, do you mean the operations organ in which you served, not the duty operations officer of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Using the information, the daily information on the developments of their day, a compilation would be made to be entered into that war journal. This is prescribed also in the manual how to keep this journal, which rubrics it should contain, and which activities it should reflect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you, by the way, are there other positions in the brigade that have some overlapping duties with the duty operations officer? Where would these other duty operations officers be situated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: There is a forward command post within the brigade which had its own duty officer, and in all subordinated units - battalions, companies subordinated to the Zvornik Brigade - there were individual duty officers. According to the manual on internal service, we had guard duty service, firefighting service, duty officers in the rolling stock department. The duty service functioned completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those days, that is, on the 12th of July, when you were the duty officer, was there also a duty officer for the barracks? Did such a position exist?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: Many attempts were made to integrate this at the level of the barracks, but in fact we had a duty officer for the brigade, not for the barracks at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the duty officer at the forward command post. Do you remember whether in those days of July a forward command post was operating and where it was located, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: The forward command post was occupied only occasionally, and it was the commander's decision when to take up position at the forward command post, who should do it, et cetera, but I don't know whether Commander Obrenovic issued such orders in that period and who, if anyone, he sent to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now ask you: If there is a forward command post and if somebody is actually there, should there also be a duty officer at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: If somebody is holding position at the forward command post, it is not necessary to have anyone on duty there serving as a duty officer. One duty officer at the brigade is enough. So we had the operations officer at the forward command post and the duty officer in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. I will not ask you any more questions about the forward command post because, in view of your engagement during those days, you are obviously not familiar with the issue. My next question would be: Does the duty operations officer have any authority, in terms of command and control, over the existing subordinated battalions of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC
utterances.text: In practice, the duty operations officer never played a commanding or controlling role in the brigade. He could receive orders from Chief of Staff or the commander and transmit those orders to the designated recipient. He could also receive orders from the Superior Command, and in that case it would be his duty to familiarise the designated recipient. However, it was not his job to inquire about the activities involved unless specifically instructed to do so in case of any feedback. But the duty operations officer could tell the driver, the messenger, or a guard to execute certain orders. He could issue orders to these people. A vehicle, for instance, could not leave the perimeter of the brigade without the approval of the Chief of Staff, let alone a unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. Let us try to specify this explanation. On the 12th and the 13th, did you as the duty operations officer have any possibility to control the artillery or the air defence, to command the intelligence organ? Was there any way for you to use your position of duty operations officer to command units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Whether this person has command authority over all these units, it's not the position in the indictment, nor the Prosecutor's position, that this is a command-authority position. I don't think there is any disagreement about the definition of "duty officer." So going into detail about whether this person could command artillery or anything is really beyond the relevance of the issues at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think there's a problem of the translation or the courtroom, you know, issue, you know. Well, maybe, Mr. Stojanovic, you could rephrase your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Maybe I should try again for the umpteenth time, for the record and to follow your suggestion, to say that my question phrased in the language understood by both me and the witness was: Was he able to - and the proper word would be - to "direct"? Not to "control," the word used in the indictment. We know that command responsibility is not among the charges in our indictment, and we are not charged under Article 7(3) of the Statute. And you know, Your Honour, that several times in the indictment it says that "Dragan Jokic directed," or, rather, "controlled." I will no longer go into these issues concerning the authority of the duty operations officer in light of the indictment. I believe that I have responded to the comment of Mr. McCloskey, if I understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I have no objections whatsoever for him questioning on terms of, you know, direct or other things that are mentioned in the indictment, of course; it's just this idea of command authority is, I think, at issue, and I think everyone understands that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Or do you want to change the subject? Maybe it's a good time for us to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I thought I would conclude with this to show exactly what our line of questioning is and what our focus of attention is concerning the position of the duty operations officer. And after that I would move to the events of the 12th and the 13th, so this would be as good a moment as any to stop for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can I give you five minutes to finish this section? If you could, so we will sit until quarter to 2.00, but if you couldn't, you know, we'll come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we shall continue tomorrow, with your leave, Your Honour, in view of my next questions which are going to concentrate on specific events of that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Witness, I have to remind you that you are still under the oath, so do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony today. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of, July, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
